"Fulfil the contracts" (﴿أَوْفُواْ بِٱلْعُقُودِ﴾). It has been said: the "contracts" here refer to the agreements a person makes with others, such as sale, marriage, manumission and the like. It has also been said: they refer to what a person has contracted with his Lord of acts of obedience, such as the Hajj, fasting and the like. And it has been said: they refer to what God has imposed upon them of permissibility and prohibition in His religion. He mentioned this in general terms and then detailed it afterwards in His words: "Lawful to you..." (﴿أُحِلَّتْ لَكُمْ﴾) and what follows.

﴿بَهِيمَةُ ٱلأَنْعَامِ﴾ ("the beast of cattle") refers to camels, cows and sheep. The attribution of "beast" (bahima) to "cattle" (an'am) is of the type of attributing a thing to what is more specific than it, because bahima applies to cattle and to other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the attribution that carries the meaning of "min" (from), like "a ring of iron" (khatam min hadid), meaning the beast consisting of cattle. It has also been said: it refers to wild animals, such as gazelles and wild cattle. The well-known usage of the Arabs is that "an'am" applies only to camels, cows and sheep, and that "bahima" applies to every animal other than man.

﴿إِلاَّ مَا يُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("except what is recited to you") means carrion and what is related to it. ﴿غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي ٱلصَّيْدِ﴾ ("not making lawful the hunting game") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "lakum" (to you). ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ ("while you are in the state of ihram") is a circumstantial state from "muhillin" (those making lawful). "Hurum" is the plural of "haram", meaning one who has entered into the state of ihram for Hajj. Thus the exception introduced by "illa" is from the lawful cattle, and the exception introduced by "ghayr" is from the people addressed.

﴿Do not violate the sacred symbols of Allah﴾. It has been said: they are the rites of the Hajj. The polytheists used to perform the Hajj and the 'Umrah, and the Muslims wanted to raid them, so it was said to them: "Do not violate the sacred symbols of Allah," meaning do not raid them and do not prevent them (from reaching the House). It has also been said: they are the sanctuary (al-Haram), and violating it is hunting in it. It has been said: they are what is forbidden to the pilgrim (muhrim) of women, perfume, hunting, and other things, and violating them is doing these. ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾. It has been said: it refers to the genus of the four sacred months, which are Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram. It has also been said: the months of the Hajj, which are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah. Violating them is fighting in them and changing their status. ﴿Nor the offering﴾, which is what is brought to the Sacred House of the livestock animals and slaughtered seeking nearness to Allah. So Allah forbade that it be violated by being raided, or by preventing (people) from the House. ﴿Nor the garlands﴾. It has been said: these are what is hung on the necks of the offering animals, so He forbade interfering with them. It has also been said: He meant the animals bearing garlands among the offerings, which are the camels (al-budn), and He mentioned them again by name after their inclusion in the offerings, to show concern for them and to emphasize their matter. ﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾, meaning those intending the House for Hajj or 'Umrah. Allah forbade raiding them or preventing them from the House. According to al-Suhayli, the verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam al-Bakri, whose name was Shurayh ibn Dubay'ah, who was seized by the horsemen of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was heading to the Ka'bah to perform 'Umrah. This prohibition on violating these things is general, covering both Muslims and polytheists. Then the prohibition on fighting the polytheists was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and by His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and by His saying: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17]. ﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord and His pleasure﴾. The bounty (al-fadl) is profit in trade, and the pleasure (al-ridwan) is mercy in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾, meaning: when you have come out of your state of ihram for Hajj, then hunt if you wish. So the command here is permission, by consensus (ijma'). ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people, because they prevented you from the Sacred Mosque, incite you to transgress﴾. The meaning of "yajrimannakum" is: "let it not earn for you" (lā yuksibannakum). It is said: "jarama fulan fulanan hadha al-amr" when he caused him to earn it and compelled him to it. Al-shana'an is hatred and enmity; it is said with the "n" vowelled or with it sukun. "An sadduhum" is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and "an ta'taduu" is the second object of "yajrimannakum". The meaning of the verse: do not let the enmity of a people lead you to transgress against them because they prevented you from the Sacred Mosque. It was revealed in the year of the Conquest, when the Muslims overcame the people of Makkah and wanted to annihilate them by killing, because they had prevented the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. So Allah forbade them from killing them, because Allah knew that they would believe. ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾, a general injunction. The difference between al-birr and al-taqwa is that al-birr is general, covering the performance of obligations and recommended acts, the abandonment of prohibitions, and everything that brings one closer to Allah, while al-taqwa concerns obligations and abandoning prohibitions without performing recommended acts. Thus al-birr is more general than al-taqwa. ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and transgression﴾. The difference between them is that sin (al-ithm) is every sin between the servant and Allah or between him and people, while transgression (al-'udwan) is against people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 3:

﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine﴾ Discussion of these has already passed in al-Baqarah [173]. ﴿And that which has been strangled﴾ is that which is choked by a rope or the like. ﴿And that which has been beaten to death﴾ is that which is struck with a stick or a stone or the like. ﴿And that which has fallen to death﴾ is that which falls from a mountain or the like. ﴿And that which has been gored﴾ is that which has been gored by another animal. ﴿And that which a beast of prey has eaten﴾, meaning it has eaten part of it. The beast of prey (al-sab') is every carnivorous animal, such as the wolf, the lion, the panther, the fox, the eagle and the vulture. ﴿Except what you have slaughtered﴾. It has been said that this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and that is when what is meant by the strangled and its companions is what died from strangling, beating, falling, goring and being eaten by a beast of prey. The meaning would then be: these things are forbidden to you, but what you slaughter from among them is lawful. This is a weak view, because if they died by these causes, they are carrion, and so they have entered under the general meaning of carrion, and there is no benefit in mentioning them afterward. It has also been said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and that is when what is meant by the strangled and its companions is what was struck by those causes but whose slaughter was still reached. The meaning according to this view is: except what you reached the slaughter of from these things, which is lawful. Then the people of this view differed as to whether it is a condition that its life-force (muqalah) has not been fully spent or not. As for when it has not come close to death from these causes, its slaughter is permissible by consensus. ﴿And what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾ is joined to the forbidden things mentioned. The nusub are stones that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to venerate and slaughter upon. They are not idols, because idols are carved in images, whereas the nusub are not carved, and they are the ansab. The singular is nisab. It has been said that nusub (with two dammas) is a singular, and its plural is ansab. ﴿And that you seek decision by the arrows﴾ is also joined to the forbidden things. Al-istiqsam is seeking what has been allotted to one. The azlam are the hassam (lots), and its singular is zalm, with the zay vowelled either with a damma or a fatha. There were three of them: on one was written "Do", on another "Do not", and the third was blank. When a person wanted to do something, he placed them in a bag, put his hand in and drew one out. If the one marked "Do" came out, he did what he intended; if the one marked "Do not" came out, he refrained; and if the blank one came out, he drew again. ﴿That is a transgression (fisq)﴾. The reference is either to the consumption of all the forbidden things mentioned, or to the seeking of decision by the arrows. Allah forbade it and made it a transgression only because it is an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen, which Allah alone possesses; it is like soothsaying and other things by which one seeks to know the unseen. ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾, meaning they despaired of overcoming it and of seeking it. It was revealed after the afternoon prayer on the Friday, the Day of Arafah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage. That is the day mentioned, because Islam became manifest in it and the Muslims became numerous; it is possible that the intended time is the present era rather than that very day. ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. This perfection may be by victory and dominance, or by teaching the laws and explaining what is lawful and unlawful. ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾ refers back to the forbidden things mentioned before this; Allah permitted them in the case of necessity. ﴿By severe hunger﴾, meaning by famine. ﴿Not inclining toward sin﴾, meaning not transgressing and not exceeding, and this has been discussed in al-Baqarah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This stands in place of "there is no sin upon him," and it includes an addition of promise.

**﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾** The occasion of its revelation is that the Muslims asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what food was lawful for them. It is also said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered the killing of dogs, they asked him, "What is lawful for us from dogs?" So it was revealed, explaining the hunting with dogs. **﴿Say: Lawful for you are the good things﴾**. According to Malik, these are the lawful things, which is what has not been prohibited in the Book or the Sunnah. According to al-Shafi'i, they are the lawful things that are agreeable to the taste, so he prohibited everything repulsive, such as beetles, frogs and the like, because they are among the **khaba'ith** (foul things).

**﴿And [what] you have taught of the trained hunting animals﴾**. This is coordinated with "the good things" by omitting a noun: the meaning is "and the game of what you have taught." Or it is a subject whose predicate is **"fakulu mimma amsakna 'alaykum"** (so eat of what they catch for you). This second view is better, because there is no disagreement about it. The **jawarih** (trained hunting animals) are dogs and similar animals used for hunting. They were called **jawarih** because they earn for their owners; it is from **al-jarh**, in the sense of earning. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of hunting with dogs. There is disagreement about other animals. The position of the majority (**jumhur**, the majority of scholars) is permissibility, based on the reports concerning hawks and others. Some scholars prohibited some of this, based on His saying **"mukallibin"**, since it is derived from **kalb** (dog).

The verse was revealed concerning 'Adi ibn Hatim, who had dogs with which he hunted, so he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what game was lawful. **﴿Mukallibin﴾** means training dogs to hunt. It is also said that its meaning is "owners of dogs," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (**hal**) from the pronoun of the agent in **'allamtum**. His saying "you have taught" and "trainers" implies that hunting is not permitted except with a trained hunting animal, due to His saying "what you have taught." His saying **"mukallibin"** according to the first view emphasizes this by His saying **"tu'allimunahunna"** (you teach them).

The limit of training according to Ibn al-Qasim is that the trained animal learns **al-ishla'** (sending it on) and **al-zajr** (restraining it). It is also said that **al-ishla'** alone is sufficient, and it is also said that **al-zajr** alone is sufficient, and it is also said that it is that it comes back when called.

**﴿You teach them from what Allah has taught you﴾**. That is, you teach them the stratagems of hunting and bringing the game. This is part of what Allah has taught mankind, so **"min"** (from) is for partition. It may also be for the beginning of the extent. The sentence is either in the position of a circumstantial clause or a new sentence.

**﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾**. The command here is for permission. It may mean by "what they catch" whether the trained animals ate from it or did not eat. This is the apparent meaning of the wording, and Malik adopted this. It may also mean what they catch and did not eat from. This was explained by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his saying: "If it eats from it, do not eat, for it has only caught for itself." Some scholars have adopted this view. It is also reported in another hadith: "If it eats, then eat," and this is evidence for Malik.

**﴿And mention the name of Allah over it﴾**. This is a command to pronounce the name of Allah over the game, and slaughter follows the same rule. People have differed about the ruling on pronouncing the name. The Zahiriyya (the literalist school) said it is obligatory, taking the command as indicating obligation; if the name is left out deliberately or through forgetfulness, the game is not eaten according to them. Al-Shafi'i said it is recommended, taking the command as indicating recommendation, and the game is eaten according to him, whether the name was left out deliberately or through forgetfulness. Some scholars made the pronoun in **"'alayhi"** refer to the eating, so there is no command in it to pronounce the name over the game according to this view. Malik's position is that if we leave out the name deliberately, the game is not eaten, and if one leaves it out through forgetfulness, it is eaten. So it is, according to him, obligatory with remembrance and dropped with forgetfulness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 5–7:

﴿Today the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ The meaning of ḥill (ḥalal, lawful) is ḥalāl. "Those who were given the Book" are the Jews and the Christians. Scholars differed concerning the Christians of the Banu Taghlib among the Arabs, and concerning one who had been a Muslim and then apostatized to Judaism or Christianity: is their food lawful for us or not? The wording of the verse requires permissibility, since they are People of the Book. Scholars also differed concerning the Magians (majus) and the Sabians: are they People of the Book or not?

As for food, it falls into three categories. The first is slaughtered animals (dhabā'ih). The scholars agreed that these are intended by the verse, so they permitted the slaughter of all Jews and Christians. They differed concerning what is forbidden to them in their own religion, whether it is lawful for us or not, with three opinions: permissibility, prohibition, and reprehensibility (karahah). This difference is based on whether "their food" means what they slaughter or what is lawful for them. If by their food is meant what they slaughter, it is permitted; if it is meant what is lawful for them, it is prohibited; and reprehensibility is a middle position between the two opinions. The second category is that in which they have no involvement, such as wheat and fruit; this is permitted for us by consensus. The third category is that in which they have some involvement, such as bread, pressing of oil, and the setting of cheese, and similar things in which impurity (najasah) may be used. Ibn 'Abbas prohibited it, because he held that their food is specifically the slaughtered animals, and because it may be impure. The majority permitted it, because they considered it included in their food. This applies when the use of impurity in it is possible. But if we are certain that impurity was used in it, such as wine, pork, or carrion, it is not permitted at all. Al-Tartushi wrote a work on the prohibition of Christian cheese and said that it renders the seller, the buyer, and the utensil impure, because they set it with the rennet of carrion. Oil is similar to this if we know that they put it in carrion containers.

﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾: this is a permission for the Muslims to feed the People of the Book from their food.

﴿And the chaste women﴾: this is a conjunction with the lawful food. It has already been stated that ihsan (chastity, marital status) has four meanings: Islam, marriage, chastity, and freedom. As for Islam, it is not valid here, because of His saying "from those who were given the Book." As for marriage, it is also not valid, because a married woman is not lawful to another. The meanings of chastity and freedom remain possible. Whoever takes it to mean chastity permits marriage to a Scripturist woman, whether she is free or a slave. Whoever takes it to mean freedom permits marriage to a free Scripturist woman and prohibits a slave woman; this is the position of Malik. There is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: "And do not marry idolatresses," because this one concerns Scripturist women and the other concerns idolatresses. Some people have held that this verse abrogates that one, and it has been said the reverse.

The meaning of ﴿give them their due compensation﴾ [al-Nisa: 24] has already been stated. As for the meaning of "takers of lovers" (akhdan): ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153]. It was revealed concerning the expedition of al-Muraysi', when the necklace of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) broke. The people remained searching for it while they were not at water and had no water with them. So the concession of tayammum was revealed. Usayd ibn Hudayr said: "This is not your first blessing, O family of Abu Bakr." Therefore this verse is called the verse of tayammum. Wudu' had been prescribed before it and was established by the Sunnah.

His saying "when you rise to prayer" means: when you intend to rise to prayer, then perform ablution. Its apparent meaning requires renewing wudu' for every prayer; this is the position of Ibn Sirin and 'Ikrimah. The position of the majority is that it is not obligatory. They differed in interpreting the verse with four opinions. First: the obligation of renewing wudu' for every prayer is abrogated by the action of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he prayed the five prayers on the day of the Conquest with one wudu'. Second: what the verse requires of renewal is to be understood as recommended. Third: its implied meaning is "when you rise in a state of minor impurity," so it is obligatory only on the one who has become impure. Fourth: its implied meaning is "when you rise from sleep."

﴿So wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾: the verse mentions four members, two with defined limits and two without. The two defined are the hands and the feet; the two undefined are the face and the head. As for the two defined limits, washing the hands up to the elbows and the feet up to the ankles is obligatory by consensus, since that is the limit Allah set for them. It was differed whether washing the elbows with the hands and the ankles with the feet is obligatory or not. This depends on the meaning of ila (to, up to). Whoever takes ila to mean "with" in His saying "up to the elbows" and "up to the ankles" makes it obligatory to wash them. Whoever takes it to mean the limit (ghayah) does not make their washing obligatory. There was also a difference about the ankles: are they the two bones at the place where the strap is tied, or the two protruding bones at the lower end of the shin? The latter is more apparent, because He mentioned them with the dual form; had He meant the bones at the strap, He would have mentioned them in the plural as He mentioned the elbows, since on that view each foot has one ankle. As for the undefined members, there is consensus on the obligation to cover the whole face. Its length is from the beginning of the hairline to the end of the chin or beard, and its breadth is from ear to ear; it has also been said: from one temple to the other. As for the head, Malik's position is that it must be covered entirely as the face is, while many scholars hold that it is permissible to suffice with part of it, based on the report that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped over his forelock. They differed, however, about the amount that suffices, with many opinions.

﴿And wipe over your heads﴾: scholars differed concerning this bā' (the "bi" in bi-ru'usikum). Some people said it is for partiality (tab'id), and built on this the permissibility of wiping only part of the head. This view is not sound according to the scholars of Arabic grammar. Al-Qarafi said it is the bā' of instrumentality (isti'anah), which enters upon tools, and that the meaning is: wipe your hands over your heads. This is weak, because on this view the head is what is wiped, not what is wiped over, which contradicts the intended meaning. It has also been said that it is extra (za'idah), which is weak, because this is not a place for its extra use. The correct view in my opinion is that it is the bā' of adhesion (ilsaq) which connects the verb to its object, because wiping is sometimes transitive by itself and sometimes with a preposition, as in His saying: "wipe with your faces" and His saying: ﴿So he began to pass his hand over the shins and necks﴾ [Sad: 33].

﴿And your feet up to the ankles﴾: it is read as "wa-arjulakum" with the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction with the faces and hands, which requires washing the feet. It is also read in the genitive (khafḍ). Some scholars interpreted it as a conjunction with "bi-ru'usikum" and permitted wiping the feet; this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The majority said wiping them is not permitted, but washing them is obligatory. They interpreted the reading in the genitive in three ways: first, that it is genitive by proximity (khafḍ 'ala al-jiwar), not by conjunction; second, that it means wiping over the leather socks (khuffayn); third, that it is abrogated by the Sunnah. The difference between washing (ghasl) and wiping (mash) is that wiping is passing the hands over the moisture remaining from water, whereas washing according to Malik is passing the hand with water, and according to al-Shafi'i is passing water, even if one does not rub with the hand.

﴿And if you are sick or on a journey﴾: its counterpart in al-Nisa has already been discussed.

﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship﴾: that is, any constriction or difficulty, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The religion of Allah is ease." The rest of the verse is a bounty from Allah upon His servants and a mercy. Within it is encouragement toward purity and stimulation toward it.

﴿And His covenant with which He bound you﴾: this is what occurred at the Pledge of al-'Aqabah and the Pledge of al-Ridwan, and every occasion in which the Muslims said: "We hear and we obey."

The wording of the verse requires permissibility, since they are People of the Book. Scholars also differed concerning the Magians (majus) and the Sabians: are they People of the Book or not?

As for food, it falls into three categories. The first is slaughtered animals (dhabā'ih). The scholars agreed that these are intended by the verse, so they permitted the slaughter of all Jews and Christians. They differed concerning what is forbidden to them in their own religion, whether it is lawful for us or not, with three opinions: permissibility, prohibition, and reprehensibility (karahah). This difference is based on whether "their food" means what they slaughter or what is lawful for them. If by their food is meant what they slaughter, it is permitted; if it is meant what is lawful for them, it is prohibited; and reprehensibility is a middle position between the two opinions. The second category is that in which they have no involvement, such as wheat and fruit; this is permitted for us by consensus. The third category is that in which they have some involvement, such as bread, pressing of oil, and the setting of cheese, and similar things in which impurity (najasah) may be used. The majority permitted it, because they considered it included in their food. This applies when the use of impurity in it is possible. But if we are certain that impurity was used in it, such as wine, pork, or carrion, it is not permitted at all. Al-Tartushi wrote a work on the prohibition of Christian cheese and said that it renders the seller, the buyer, and the utensil impure, because they set it with the rennet of carrion. Oil is similar to this if we know that they put it in carrion containers.

﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice﴾: the discussion of its counterpart in Surat al-Nisa' has already been given. ﴿And do not let hatred of a people prompt you to deviate from justice﴾: that is, let not the enmity of a people lead you to abandon justice concerning them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 11:

﴿When a people intended to stretch out their hands against you⁠—﴾ Concerning its occasion there are four opinions. The first: the Prophet (ﷺ) went to the Banu al-Nadir of the Jews, and they resolved to drop a boulder upon him to kill him with it, so Jibril informed him of that and he rose from the place. What strengthens this opinion is what comes after this verse concerning the treachery of the Jews. The second: it was revealed concerning the Bedouin who drew his sword against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he found him on a journey, alone, and said to him, "Who will protect you from me?" He said, "Allah." So he sheathed the sword and sat down. His name was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith al-Muharibi al-Ghatafani. The third: it concerns what the disbelievers intended of attacking the Muslims when the prayer of fear was revealed. The fourth: it is in general, concerning Allah's repelling of the disbelievers from the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 12–13:

﴿ٱثْنَيْ عَشَرَ نَقِيباً﴾ "The naqib (chief/leader) is the elder of the people who is in charge of their affairs." ﴿إِنِّي مَعَكُمْ﴾ means "with My help," and the address is to the Children of Israel. It is said that the address is to the nuqaba' (chiefs).

﴿يُحَرِّفُونَ ٱلْكَلِمَ﴾ Scholars differed: is what is meant the distortion of the wording or of the meanings?

﴿وَلاَ تَزَالُ تَطَّلِعُ عَلَىٰ خَآئِنَةٍ مِّنْهُمْ﴾ means "you will not cease to discover treachery among them," so khā'ina is a verbal noun like al-'aqiba. It is said that it means "on a treacherous group among them," and this is a report about a future matter.

﴿فَٱعْفُ عَنْهُمْ﴾ Abrogated (mansukh) by the sword and the jizya (poll-tax).

"Min alladhina" is connected to "akhadhna mithaqahum" (We took their covenant), and the pronoun refers back to the Christians. "Fa-aghrayna" (﴿فَأَغْرَيْنَا﴾) means We caused to cling and We fastened, and it is derived from al-ighra' (incitement, instigating enmity).

"O People of the Scripture" in both places includes the Jews and the Christians. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Jews who were in Medina, for they used to mention the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). In the verse there is an indication of the truth of his prophethood, because he made clear to them what they had concealed from what was in their books, while he was unlettered and had not read their books. ﴿And pardons much⦆ meaning: he leaves it aside and does not expose you for it. ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book⦆ — the light is Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Book is the Qur'an.

﴿Say: "Who then has any power against God in anything?"﴾ (al-ayah): A refutation of those who said that God is Jesus, a sect of the Christians. ﴿He creates what He wills﴾: an indication of His creating Jesus without a father.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 18:**

﴿And the Jews and the Christians said﴾ — meaning: each sect said of itself that they are the sons of God and His beloved ones. The sonship here is the sonship of tenderness and compassion. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, "We are the followers of the sons of God in their view, and they are al-Masih and 'Uzayr, just as the retinue of kings say, 'We are the kings.'" ﴿Then why does He punish you?﴾ This is a rebuttal to them, since they themselves acknowledged that they would enter the Fire for a number of countable days. The Sufis have derived from the verse that the lover does not punish his beloved, and in that there is good news for whoever God loves.

ﷻ﴿وَجَعَلَكُمْ مُّلُوكاً﴾ It was said: He made among you kings, meaning rulers (umara’). It was also said: "king" is one who has a dwelling, a wife, and a servant. ﴿مَّا لَمْ يُؤْتِ أَحَداً مِّن ٱلْعَٱلَمِينَ﴾ It was said: this means the manna, the quails, the cloud, and other signs. On this view, "the worlds" is specific to the people of their own time, because the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been given the like of such signs and greater than them. It was also said: what is meant is the great number of prophets. On this view, "the worlds" is general, because there were more prophets among the Children of Israel than among all other nations.

"The Holy Land": the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is said also: Mount Sinai (al-Tur), and it is said: Damascus. ﴿Which God has prescribed for you﴾, i.e., decreed that it be yours. ﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾: this may mean apostasy from the religion and from obedience, and returning to the road by which they had come. For it is narrated that when Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them to enter the Holy Land, they feared the tyrants (al-Jabbarin) who were in it, and they resolved to appoint a leader for themselves and return to Egypt. ﴿A people of tyrants﴾: they are the Amalekites. ﴿Two men said﴾: they are Yusha' (Joshua) and Kalib (Caleb). ﴿Who feared﴾: i.e., they feared God. It is said: they feared the tyrants, but God bestowed upon them patience and steadfastness because of the sincerity of their faith. ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾: i.e., the gate of the city. ﴿So go you and your Lord﴾: an extreme in disobedience and bad manners, with an expression that implies disbelief and contempt for God and His Messenger. It is said: it is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "la amliku" (I do not possess): meaning, I do not possess except myself, and my brother does not possess except himself. It is also said: it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, i.e., "my brother does not possess except himself." ﴿So part You between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾: i.e., separate between us and them, so it is from separation (furqah). It is said: judge between us and them with a decision.

﴿He said: "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years."﴾ The pronoun in "qala" (he said) refers to Allah, the Exalted. Allah forbade all the Children of Israel to enter that city for forty years, and He left them during this period wandering in the land, meaning the land of wandering (al-tih), which lies between Egypt and Syria (al-Sham), until everyone who had said, "We will never enter it," had died. None of that generation entered it except Yusha' (Joshua) and Kalib (Caleb). Harun (Aaron) died during the wandering, and Musa (Moses) died after him, also during the wandering.

It has been said that Musa and Harun were not in the wandering, based on His words: ﴿So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ Yusha' led the Children of Israel out after the forty years, fought the giants (al-Jabbarin), and conquered the city.

The governing element (al-'amil) for "forty" is "muharramah" (forbidden), according to the default reading (al-asl), so it must be connected to what precedes it. It has also been said that the governing element is "yatihun" (they wander). On this view, it is permissible to pause (al-waqf) at His words "muharramah 'alayhim" (forbidden to them). This view is weak, because there is no reason to front the governed element here, and also because the first view is fuller in meaning, since it explains the duration of the prohibition and the wandering.

﴿They wander﴾, meaning they become bewildered. It is narrated that they would travel all night, but when they woke in the morning they found themselves at the same place where they had been.

﴿So do not grieve﴾, meaning do not be sad. The address is to Musa, and it has also been said that it is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). By "the defiantly disobedient" is meant the Jews who were in his time.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 27:

﴿The story of the two sons of Adam﴾ They are Qabil (Cain) and Habil (Abel). ﴿When they both offered an offering﴾ It is related that Qabil was a man who worked the land, and he offered the worst of his crops. Habil was a man who kept sheep, and he offered the best ram he had. The custom at that time was that a person would bring his offering near to God and then stand and pray. If a fire came down from the sky and consumed the offering, that was a sign of its acceptance; otherwise it was not accepted. The fire came down, took the ram of Habil, lifted it up, and left the crop of Qabil. So Qabil envied him and killed him. ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from those who are mindful of Him﴾ The Mu'tazilah and others have used this as evidence that the deeds of a person who commits sins are not accepted. The Ash'aris interpreted it to mean that the "taqwa" (God-consciousness) here refers to taqwa of shirk (associating partners with God).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 28–31:

﴿Even if you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you﴾ (the verse). It has been said: its meaning is, if you initiate fighting against me, I shall not initiate it against you. And it has been said: if you initiate fighting against me, I shall not defend myself against you. Then scholars differed over this view: was his leaving off defense of himself out of scrupulousness (tawarru') and virtue (fadilah)? This is the more evident and better-known view. It was obligatory for them that no one defend himself, and this is the opinion of Mujahid. As for our law (shari'ah), a person may defend himself, and indeed it is obligatory. ﴿Indeed, I wish that you bear my sin and your sin﴾. The "wish" (iradah) here is not a wish of love and desire, but rather a choice of the lesser of two evils, as if he said: if you kill me, that is more beloved to me than that I kill you, as is reported in the narration: "Be the slain servant of God, and do not be the slaying servant of God." As for his words "with my sin and your sin," its meaning is: with the sin of my killing you had I killed you, and with the sin of your killing me. The killer bears both sins, because he is the wrongdoer. This is like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The two who revile each other bear the sin of what they said," meaning it falls upon the one who initiates. It has also been said: "with my sin" means you bear my other sins on my behalf, because on the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer is made to carry the sins of the wronged. "With your sin" means with your sin of killing me, and with your other sins. ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾. It may be from the speech of Habil, or it may be a resumed statement from the speech of God Most High. ﴿Then God sent a crow﴾ (the verse). It is reported that two crows fought until one killed the other, then the killer began searching for earth and covering the dead one. It has also been said that it was a single crow that searched and cast earth upon Habil. ﴿The shame of his brother﴾, meaning his private part (awrah), and it was singled out for mention because covering it is more important than covering the rest of the body. The pronoun in "his brother" refers to the son of Adam. It appears from this story that Habil was the first of the children of Adam to be buried. ﴿He said: "Woe is me!"﴾ The original is "ya waylati," then the yaʼ was replaced by an alif, and the taʼ was vocalized with a fatha, and likewise "ya asafa" and "ya hasratan." ﴿And he became among the regretful﴾ over what he had done of killing his brother. Scholars differed over whether Qabil was a disbeliever or a sinner. The sound view is that he was not a disbeliever during that period, because he intended to draw near to God through the offering. "Asbaha" here and elsewhere is an expression for all times, not restricted to the morning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 32:

﴿Because of that﴾ relates to "We prescribed" (kataba). It was also said that it relates to "the regretful" (al-nadimin), but this is weak. ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾, meaning we made it obligatory upon them, or We wrote it in their scriptures. ﴿That whoever kills a soul, unless it be for a soul or for corruption in the land﴾, meaning without him having killed a soul for which retaliation (qisas) is due, ﴿or corruption in the land﴾, meaning a corruption for which killing becomes obligatory, such as highway robbery (hirabah). ﴿It is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾. This is a figure of speech: the killing of one being equated with the killing of all can be conceived from three aspects. The first is retaliation (qisas), for the retaliation for killing one person and for killing all is the same. The second is the violation of the sanctity and the rushing into disobedience. The third is sin and the punishment of the Hereafter. Mujahid said: God has promised the one who kills a soul Hell and abiding in it, and wrath, curse and a great punishment. So if he killed all people he would not receive more than that. This aspect is the most apparent, because the purpose of the verse is to magnify the killing of a soul and to emphasise its gravity so that people will refrain from it. Likewise the reward for preserving a life is like the reward for preserving all lives, in order to magnify the matter and encourage it. Preserving a life means rescuing it from death, such as rescuing someone from fire or drowning or the like. It was also said: it means refraining from killing it, and it was said: it means pardoning when retaliation has become due. ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾: the pronoun refers to the Children of Israel. The meaning is the censure of their deeds, and in this is an indication of what they intended regarding the killing of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 5, verses 33–34:

﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war﴾ etc. Its occasion of revelation, according to Ibn ʿAbbas: a people of the Jews had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant and cut off the road. A group said it was revealed concerning a number of people from ʿUkl and ʿUrayna who had outwardly embraced Islam; then they killed the shepherd of the Prophet (ﷺ) and took his camels. Its ruling was afterwards applied to every muharib (one who wages armed robbery, or brigandage, against people). According to Malik, al-muharabah (armed aggression, or brigandage, the waging of war) is: carrying weapons against people, whether in a town or outside a town. Abu Hanifa said: the muharib is only one who acts outside the town.

His saying ﴿wage war against Allah﴾ is an intensification and an exaggeration. Some of them said its meaning is: they wage war against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but this is weak, because the Messenger (ﷺ) is mentioned afterwards. It was also said: they wage war against the servants of Allah, and this is better.

﴿and strive upon the earth in corruption﴾ explains al-hirabah, and it has degrees: the lowest of them is frightening the road, then taking property, then killing a soul.

﴿that they be killed or crucified﴾: crucifixion (al-salb) is joined to killing. It was said: he is killed and then crucified so that the people of corruption see it and desist. This is the view of Ashhab. It was also said: he is crucified alive and killed on the wood. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim.

﴿or their hands and their feet be cut off from opposite sides﴾: its meaning is that his right hand and left foot are cut off. Then, if he returns, his left hand and right foot are cut off. The cutting of the hand, according to Malik and the majority, is from the wrist, and the cutting of the foot is from the joint. This applies to hirabah and to theft.

﴿or they be exiled from the land﴾: the well-known position of Malik's school is that he is banished from one town to another town and imprisoned there until his repentance appears. Mutarrif narrated from him that he is imprisoned in the same town itself, and Abu Hanifa said likewise. It was also said: he is exiled to another town without being imprisoned there.

The school of Malik holds that the imam has discretion regarding the muharib between: killing him and crucifying him, or killing him without crucifying him, or cutting off his hand and foot, or exiling him. Yet he said: if he has killed, then he must be killed; and if he has not killed, then it is best to apply the lightest of the punishments to him.

Al-Shafiʿi and others said: these punishments are ordered (graded). Whoever kills and takes property is killed and crucified; whoever kills and does not take property is killed and not crucified; whoever takes property and does not kill has his hand and foot cut off; and whoever frightens the road without killing and without taking property is exiled.

Malik's proof is that these punishments are joined by ﴿or﴾ (aw), which implies choice.

﴿A disgrace for them in this world﴾: it is the punishment, and the torment of the Hereafter. The apparent meaning of this is that punishment in this world does not serve as expiation (kaffarah) for the muharib, unlike the other hudud. It is possible that the disgrace in this world is for the one who is punished in it, and the torment in the Hereafter is for the one who is punished (there) (?).

﴿except those who repent before you have power over them, so know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: it was said: this refers to the polytheists, and this is weak, because the ruling on the repentance of a polytheist does not differ whether it is before or after one has power over him. It was said: it refers to the Muslim muharibun, and this is the correct view. They are those to whom the mentioned punishments apply. Whoever of them repents before he is captured, the ruling of hirabah falls from him, by His saying: ﴿so know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Scholars differed as to whether he is held to account for what is due to people regarding blood and property, or not. The reasoning for holding him to it is that these are additional to the hadd of hirabah, which has fallen from him by repentance. The reasoning for dropping them is the unrestricted wording of His saying: ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 35–37:

﴿And seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him﴾, meaning: that by which one seeks nearness to Him and draws close to Him, such as righteous deeds, supplication, and other things. ﴿That they may ransom themselves therewith﴾. If it is said: why is the pronoun in the singular when two things have been mentioned, namely "in the earth" and "and the like of it"? The answer is that the singular has been placed in the position of the dual, and the pronoun has been treated like a demonstrative, as if he had said: "that they may ransom themselves with that." Or the waw may be in the sense of "with," meaning "together with." ﴿A lasting punishment﴾, meaning: enduring. Likewise, "lasting bliss" (naʿīm muqīm).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 38–40:

﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾ The generality of the verse requires the cutting off of every thief. However, the jurists stipulated conditions for the cutting off (of the hand), by which they restricted the generality. Among these: one who was driven by hunger to theft is not cut off according to Malik, because carrion has been made lawful for him; likewise one who steals the property of his father or his master; or one who steals from a place that is not guarded (ḥirz) [a protected place]; or one who steals less than the minimum (niṣāb), which according to Malik is a quarter of a dinar of gold, or three dirhams of silver, or what is worth one of them. The evidences for restricting the verse by these matters are found in other verses. It has been said that the condition of ḥirz (safe custody) is derived from this verse, because what is left without guarding, or entrusted to someone, is not theft when taken; rather it is embezzlement (ikhtilas) or breach of trust (khiyana). As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of "the thief": according to Sibawayh it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, as if he had said, "What is recited to you is: the thief, male and female." According to al-Mubarrad and others, the predicate is "cut off their hands," and the fa' (then) entered because the clause includes the meaning of a conditional (sharṭ).

﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾ (the verse): The repentance of the thief is that he regrets what has passed, abandons (the sin) in what is to come, and returns what he stole to the one who is entitled to it. It is disputed: if he repents before reaching the ruler (ḥākim), does the cutting off fall from him? This is the position of al-Shafi'i, based on the apparent meaning of the verse. Or does it not fall from him? This is the position of Malik, because according to him the hudud are not waived by repentance except for the highway robber (muḥārib), due to the explicit text concerning him.

﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ The punishment is mentioned before forgiveness because it is matched with the preceding of the theft over the repentance.

O Messenger (the Prophet ﷺ): this is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, intended as consolation. ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths﴾ are the hypocrites (munafiqun). ﴿And among those who became Jews﴾ may be a conjunction with "those who said, 'We believe'," and then "listeners" (samma'un) is a new sentence (isti'naf, a resumed statement) informing about the two groups, the hypocrites and the Jews. It may also be that "among those who became Jews" is a separate new sentence cut off from what precedes, and "listeners" refers to them specifically. ﴿Listeners for another people﴾ means listeners to the words of other people from among the Jews who do not come to the Prophet ﷺ, because of their extreme hatred and their open enmity. So his saying "who have not come to you" is a description (sifah) of "another people." The "other people" are the Jews of Khaybar, and "the listeners to falsehood" are the Banu Qurayza. ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [An-Nisa: 46], meaning they change them after they have been placed in their position, and they aim them away from their correct meanings. This is a characteristic of the Jews. ﴿They say, "If you are given this, take it"﴾. It was revealed because a Jewish man committed adultery with a Jewish woman. The Jews were asked by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the punishment for the adulterer according to their law. They said: "We flog them and blacken their faces (tahmim)." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "In the Torah there is stoning (rajm)." They denied this, so he told them to bring the Torah and read it. One of them put his hand over the verse of stoning, and Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: "Lift your hand." He lifted it, and there was the verse of stoning. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then ordered that the Jewish man and the Jewish woman be stoned. So the meaning of their saying, "If you are given this, take it," is: if you are given this that you mentioned, namely flogging and blackening the face with tar, then take it and act upon it; but if you are not given it, and Muhammad ﷺ gives you a ruling other than it, then beware. ﴿His trial﴾, meaning his misguidance in this world or his punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿In this world there is disgrace﴾: humiliation, poverty (maskanah), and the jizya (poll tax).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 42–43:

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾ If the first (occurrence) refers to the Jews, then he repeats it here for emphasis; and if the first refers to the hypocrites and the Jews, then this one refers to the Jews specifically. ﴿Devourers of what is unlawful﴾, i.e., of the unlawful (ḥarām) gains, such as bribery, usury and the like. ﴿So judge between them or turn away from them﴾. This is an option given to the Prophet ﷺ: to judge between the Jews or to leave them. It also applies to the judge in general. It has been said that it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. ﴿And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the ruling of Allah?﴾ This is an expression of astonishment at their making the Prophet ﷺ their judge while they do not believe in him, and while they oppose the ruling of the Torah, which they claim to believe in. So the meaning of ﴿then they turn away after that﴾ is: they turn away from following the ruling of Allah in the Torah, after the ruling of Allah being present among them and known, in the matter of stoning and other things. ﴿And they are not believers﴾, meaning: they do not believe in the Torah and in Moses, peace be upon him. This is a reproach to them, because whoever opposes the Book of Allah and alters it, his claim to believe in it is false.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 44:

﴿The Prophets, who submitted (aslamu)﴾ are the prophets who came between Musa and Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning of "aslamu" here is "sincerely devoted to Allah" (akhlasu li-Allah). It is a phrase of praise, intended as an indirect reproach to the Jews, since they are contrary to this quality. The meaning here is not Islam in the sense that is the opposite of disbelief (kufr), because the prophets are not described as "aslamu" in that sense, as they never disbelieved at all. Rather it is like the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾, and the words of the Most High: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾.

﴿for those who were Jews (lilladhina hadu)﴾ is connected to "yahkumu" (judge), meaning: the prophets judge by the Torah for those who were Jews, and they compel them to follow it. It is also connected to his words in it "is guidance and light."

﴿by what they were entrusted with (bima istuhfizu)﴾ means they were charged with preserving it. The "ba" here indicates causation, as stated by al-Zamakhshari. It is possible that it is a substitute for the genitive noun in his words "judge by it."

﴿So do not fear the people﴾ and what follows is an address to the Jews. It may be an injunction to the Muslims, intended as an indirect reproach to the Jews, because this is among their deeds.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. Ibn Abbas said: the three (descriptions) were revealed concerning the Jews: "the disbelievers," "the wrongdoers," and "the defiantly disobedient." Traditions have been related on this from the Prophet (ﷺ). A group said: it is general, covering everyone who does not judge by what Allah has revealed, among the Jews, the Muslims and others, except that disbelief with regard to the Muslims is disbelief of disobedience (kufr ma'siyah), which does not take them out of faith. Al-Shafi'i said: "the disbelievers" refers to the Muslims, "the wrongdoers" to the Jews, and "the defiantly disobedient" to the Christians.

**[Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 5, verse 45]**

﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾: *kataba* (كتبنا) means either writing on the tablets, or obligating and imposing. The pronoun in *ʿalayhim* (عليهم) refers to the Children of Israel, and the pronoun in *fīhā* (فيها) refers to the Torah. ﴿that the life is for life﴾: that is, a person is killed if he has killed a person. This is a report about what is in the Torah, and it is a ruling in our law by *ijmāʿ* (consensus of the scholars). However, this wording is general, and the scholars have specified some exceptions to it. Mālik said: a believer is not killed for an unbeliever, because of the hadith reported on this matter, and a free person is not killed for a slave, because of His saying, "the free for the free and the slave for the slave." The discussion of this has already preceded in al-Baqarah [178]. ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ and what follows it is the ruling on *qiṣāṣ* (retaliation) for limbs. The reading with the accusative on *al-ʿayn* (العين) and what follows it is coordinated with *al-nafs* (النفس). It was also read with the nominative, and it has three possible readings: the first is coordination with the position of *al-nafs*, since the meaning is "We said to them: a life for a life." The second is coordination with the pronoun in the predicate, which is *bi-l-nafs* (بالنفس). The third is that it is a new sentence, nominative as the subject. ﴿and wounds are subject to retribution﴾: with the accusative, *al-judūḥ* (الجروح) is coordinated with the accusative items before it. With the nominative, it follows the three possibilities mentioned for the nominative of *al-ʿayn*. This wording is general, but what is meant by it is specific: the wounds from which there is no fear for the life. ﴿But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾: there are two interpretations. The first: whoever among the rightful claimants forgoes retaliation and pardons it, that is an expiation for him, and God expiates his sins for his pardon and his relinquishing of his right. The second: whoever forgives and pardons it, it is an expiation for the killer or the wounder, through God's pardon of him in that matter, because the person with the right has pardoned him. So the pronoun in *lahu* (له) on the first interpretation refers to the one who forgoes, namely the one who gives up the retaliation for the one killed or wounded, or the guardian. On the second interpretation it refers to the killer or the wounder, even though he has not been mentioned, but the context of the speech requires it. The first is more preferred, because the pronoun returns to something mentioned, which is *man* (من). Its meaning is one on both interpretations, and *ṣadaqah* (الصدقة) means pardon on both interpretations. However, the first interpretation explains the reward of the one who pardons and encourages pardon, while the second explains the removal of sin from the killer or the wounder when he is pardoned.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 46–48:

﴿Confirming what was before it﴾. The meaning of "muṣaddiq" (confirming) has already been explained in al-Baqarah. "What was before it" means the Torah, because it came before it. The Qur'an confirms the Torah and the Injil, because they came before it. "Confirming" is in apposition to the position of the phrase "in it is guidance and light," because it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿And a guardian over it﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said it means a witness, and it was said it means a trustee. ﴿Over what has come to you of the truth﴾: the statement includes the meaning of "not turning away" or "not deviating," and for this reason it takes "ʿan" (from). ﴿For each of you We have made a law (shir'ah) and a way (minhaj)﴾: [Ibn ʿAbbas said] a path and a custom. The address is to the prophets, peace be upon them, or to the nations. The meaning is that Allah made for every community a law (sharīʿah) that they follow. Those who said that the law of those before us is not a law for us have taken evidence from this, and that applies to the rulings and the subsidiary matters. As for belief (iʿtiqād), the religion in it is one for all the worlds, and it is faith in Allah, His Oneness, belief in His messengers, and faith in the Last Abode. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: some people used it as evidence that giving precedence to obligatory acts over delaying them is better, and this is agreed upon in all acts of worship except the prayer (ṣalāh), where there is a difference of opinion. The school of al-Shafiʿi holds that performing it at the beginning of its time is better, while Abu Hanifa held the opposite. In the school of Malik there is difference and detail, and they agreed that performing the Maghrib prayer early is better.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 51:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ Its occasion of revelation was the alliance of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul with the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa, and ʿUbada ibn al-Samit's renunciation of the alliance that had existed between him and them. Its wording is general, and its ruling remains in effect. It does not include dealings with them in buying, selling and the like. ﴿Indeed, he is one of them﴾ is an intensification of the threat. Whoever holds their belief is one of them in every respect, and whoever opposes them in their belief but loves them is one of them in incurring the hatred of Allah and deserving punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 52:

﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ They are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), and what is meant here is ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, who allies himself with the Jews, relies on them in large numbers, and says: "I am a man who fears misfortunes." ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him﴾ The conquest (al-fath) here is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and "a command from Him" is the destruction of the enemies by a command from Him that involves no means through any creature, or a command from Allah to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, to kill the Jews. ﴿So they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful﴾ The pronoun in "fa-yusbihu" (so they will become) refers to the hypocrites, and what they concealed was their intention to seek the help of the Jews against the Muslims and to harbor enmity toward the Muslims.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 53:

﴿And those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾ It is read as "yaqūlu" (say) without a waw, as a resumption and a statement (isti'nāf wa ikhbār). It is also read with a waw and with a raised ending (ḍamm), which is the conjunction of one sentence to another (ʿaṭf jumla ʿalā jumla). And it is read with a waw and with a fatḥa (naṣb), as a conjunction to "an yaʾtiya Allāh" (that Allah may bring), or as a conjunction to "fa-yuṣbiḥū" (so they will become).

﴿Are these the ones who swore﴾: the demonstrative refers to the hypocrites, because they used to swear that they were with the believers. The phrase "jahda aymānihim" (with their most emphatic oaths) is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad).

﴿Their deeds have become void﴾: this may be the speech of the believers, or the speech of Allah, and it may be an invocation (duʿāʾ) or a statement (khabar).

﴿Whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾: This is an address in the form of warning and threat. It also informs of the apostasy (riddah) of some Muslims, so it is a report of the unseen before it occurred. Then it happened: during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima al-Kadhdhab, apostatized, and so did Banu Mudlij, the people of al-Aswad al-Ansi, who claimed prophethood and was killed during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Banu Asad, the people of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood and then embraced Islam and struggled in jihad, also apostatized. Then the apostates multiplied and their affair spread after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), until Allah sufficed the Muslims against them through the hand of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). The tribes that apostatized after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were seven: Banu Fazara, Ghatafan, Banu Sulaym, Banu Yarbu', Kinda, Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il, and some of Banu Tamim. Then Ghassan apostatized in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, namely the people of Jabala ibn al-Ayham, who became Christian because of the slap (he received).

﴿Then Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him﴾: It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it and said: "They are a people of this one," meaning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. The indication of this, and Allah knows best, is to the people of Yemen, because the Ash'aris are from the people of Yemen. It was also said: the intended ones are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his companions who fought the people of apostasy. This is strengthened by what appeared from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) of earnestness in fighting them and determination upon it, when some people disagreed with him on that. His resolve grew firm until they agreed with him and unanimously accepted it, and Allah gave them victory over the people of apostasy. This is further strengthened by the fact that the attributes by which these people are described are the attributes of Abu Bakr. Do you not see His saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, stern toward the disbelievers﴾? Abu Bakr was weak in himself and strong in Allah. Likewise His saying: ﴿and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ refers to whoever opposed Abu Bakr and blamed him for fighting the people of apostasy, but he did not turn back from his resolve.

﴿humble (أذلة) toward the believers﴾: It is like His saying: ﴿stern (أشداء) against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (al-Fath: 29). The word أذلة was followed by عَلَى (ʿalā) only because it implies the meaning of kindness and tenderness (العطف والحنو), so it takes the preposition as if it were used in that sense.

If it is asked: where is the response (جواب) linked to the condition (شرط)? The answer: there is an omitted element, its estimated form being: "Whoever of you turns back from his religion, then Allah will bring in their place a people, or a people who will fight them."

The verse begins: ﴿Your only guardian is Allah﴾. He mentioned the guardian (al-wali) in the singular, to make Allah alone the guardian in this sense. Then He joined the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers to His name by way of following (al-tabaʿ, subordinate attachment). Had He said "your guardians are only..." the speech would have lacked a principal (asl) and a follower (tabaʿ). ﴿And they bow in prayer﴾. It is said that it was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when a beggar asked him while he was bowing in prayer, and he gave him his ring. It is also said that the verse is general. The mention of bowing after prayer is because it is among the noblest of its acts. The conjunction "wa" (and) is the "wa" of circumstance (wawu al-hal) according to the first view, and the "wa" of coordination (lil-ʿatf) according to the second.

﴿Then indeed the party of Allah﴾. This is the placing of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (iqamat al-zahir maqam al-mudmar), meaning: then indeed they are the victorious. ﴿And the disbelievers﴾ is in the accusative (bi-l-nasb) as a coordination with "those who took", and it was read in the genitive (bi-l-khafd) as a coordination with "those who were given the Book". The reading of Ibn Masʿud supports this: "and from among the disbelievers". By them are meant the polytheists among the Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 58–59:

﴿And when you call to the prayer (ṣalāh), they take it as a mockery and a jest.﴾ The verse: It is related that a man of the Christians in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," would say: "May God burn the liar." Then fire fell upon his house and he and his family were burned. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence that the adhān (call to prayer) is established from the Qur'an. ﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ He made their lack of intellect the cause of their mockery of the religion. ﴿Say: "Do you find fault with us for anything except that we believe in God and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ That is: do you criticize us or object to us except for our belief in God, His books and His messengers? That is a matter that is neither to be denied nor reproached. A parallel to this in the striking exception is the saying of al-Nābigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords
are, with them, notched from the clashing of battalions."

The verse was revealed concerning Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab, Nāfi' ibn Abī Nāfi', and a group of Jews, who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the messengers in whom he believes. He recited: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us..." until the end of the verse. When he mentioned Jesus, they said: "We do not believe in Jesus or in anyone who believed in him." ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient (fāsiqūn)﴾ It is said: it is conjoined with "we believe." It is said: it is conjoined with "what was sent down to us." It is said: it is a causal clause conjoined to an omitted causal clause, its meaning being: "Do you find fault with us only because of your lack of fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient?" It may also be that "and that most of you" is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its meaning being: "your defiant disobedience is known" or "is established."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 60:

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from Allah?"﴾ When He mentioned that the People of the Book reproach the Muslims for believing in Allah and His messengers, He mentioned the defects of the People of the Book in response to that, as a rebuttal to them. The address in "unabbi'ukum" (shall I inform you) is to the Jews, and the reference in "dhalika" (that) is to what preceded concerning the state of the believers. ﴿Recompense (mathubah) with Allah﴾: it is from "thawab" (reward), and placing "thawab" in the position of "iqab" (punishment) is a mockery of them, like their saying: "So give them the good news of a painful punishment." ﴿Those whom Allah has cursed﴾: meaning the Jews. "Man" (those who) is in the position of the nominative, as the predicate of an elided subject, its estimate being: "it is those whom Allah has cursed"; or it is in the position of the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for "sharr" (worse). There must be an elided genitive (mudaf) in the sentence, its estimate being: "worse [of those who belong to] that," and its estimate being: "the religion of those whom Allah has cursed." ﴿And He made of them apes and swine﴾: a group of the Jews were transformed into apes when they transgressed on the Sabbath, and a group of them were transformed into swine when they denied Jesus son of Mary. ﴿And who worshipped the Taghut﴾: the reading with a fatha on the "ba'" (ʿabada) is a verb conjoined to "la'anahu Allah" (whom Allah cursed). It was also read with a damma on the "ba'" and a kasra on "al-Taghut" (ʿubd al-Taghut), so that "ʿabd" is a noun in the intensive form (ʿal-mubalagha), like "yaqud," and is made genitive by its annexation to "al-Taghut." It was also read as "wa-ʿabid" and "wa-ʿabbad," and in all these readings it is conjoined to "al-qiradah wa-al-khanazir" (the apes and swine). ﴿Worse in place﴾: i.e., in standing. The attribution of "worse" to the place, while in reality it belongs to its people, is an intensification in censure.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 61–63:

﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾ It was revealed concerning hypocrites among the Jews. ﴿And they have certainly entered with disbelief﴾ Its implied sense: "while they were characterized by disbelief." The meaning is: they entered as disbelievers and they left as disbelievers. The particle qad (قد) was introduced before "entered" and "left" to bring the past closer to the present state, meaning: this was their condition in their entering and their leaving, continually. ﴿sin (al-ithm)﴾ means lying and all other disobediences. ﴿transgression (al-'udwan)﴾ means injustice. ﴿unlawful gain (al-suht)﴾ means the forbidden. ﴿Why do the rabbis and scholars not forbid them﴾ ("lawla" here) is an expression of reproach, urging and rebuke. ﴿Wretched is what they have been doing﴾ The lam in both places is the lam of oath.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 64:

﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained up."﴾ Chained hand (ghull al-yad) is a metaphor for stinginess, and extending the hand (bast al-yad) is a metaphor for generosity. From this is the verse: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾: that is, do not be utterly stingy, and do not be utterly extravagant in giving. It is narrated that the Jews were struck by a year of hardship, and so they made this shameful statement. The one who said it was Finhas, but it was attributed to the Jews in general, because they approved of his words. ﴿Their hands are chained up﴾: this may be a supplication or a statement of fact, and it may refer to this world or the Hereafter. If it refers to this world, it may mean stinginess, or it may mean their hands being chained in captivity. If it refers to the Hereafter, it means that chains will be placed upon them in Hell. ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾: a metaphor for His bounty and generosity. The two hands are mentioned in the dual here, while the singular was used in the Jews' statement "the hand of Allah is chained up," in order to refute them and to emphasize His generosity in description, like the Arab saying: "So-and-so gives with both his hands" when he is greatly generous. ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾: kindling the fire is a metaphor for attempting war, and extinguishing it is a metaphor for their being humiliated and failing to achieve victory. It may be that this refers to their forefathers, or to those among them who were contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ, and those who come after them. In that case it is a report of the unseen and good news for the Muslims.

﴿Had the People of the Book believed﴾ (the verse continues): It is possible that this refers to their earlier generations and to those who were contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ. On this reading, it is an encouragement to them to believe and to be God-conscious. ﴿And had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ means upholding them through knowledge and action. The mention of the Gospel is evidence that the Christians are included in the term Ahl al-Kitab (People of the Book). ﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾. It was said: "from above them" is an expression for rain, and "from beneath their feet" is an expression for plants and crops. It was also said that this is an isti'arah (metaphor) for expanding provision in every way. ﴿A moderate community﴾, that is, upright, and what is meant by it are those among them who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam. It was also said that it refers to those who did not oppose the earlier Prophets.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 67:

﴿O Messenger, proclaim what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾. He is commanded to convey all that was revealed to him, completely and fully, for he had already conveyed it; rather, he is commanded here not to hold back from anything out of fear of anyone. ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾. This is a warning on the assumption of failing to convey. Regarding the connection between this condition and its response, there are two opinions. The first is that the meaning is: if you leave out any part of it, it is as though you had conveyed nothing, and what you have conveyed is not counted; so the meaning of "if you do not" is: if you do not convey it in full and complete form. The second is that the meaning is: if you do not convey the message, the one who concealed it deserves punishment, and the cause is placed in the position of the effect. ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. This is a promise and a guarantee of protection. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to fear his enemies and take precautions against them in his military campaigns and elsewhere. So when this verse was revealed, he said: "O people, disperse, for Allah has protected me," and he abandoned taking precautions.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 68:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything﴾ — the verse continues — meaning: you are not upon a religion that is considered valid and called "something," ﴿until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Among establishing them is belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). And His saying: ﴿and what has been revealed to you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the Qur'an. The verse was revealed concerning Rafi' ibn Harithah, Salam ibn Mushkam, Rafi' ibn Khuzaymah, and others of the Jews who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, "We follow the Torah and do not follow anything other than it, and we do not believe in you nor follow you."

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on Surah 5, verse 69 (*al-Tashil*):

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews﴾. The discussion of its counterpart in al-Baqarah [2:62] has already passed.

﴿And the Sabians﴾. The reading of the Seven (*al-qira'at al-sab'a*, the seven canonical readings) is with the *waw* (وَ), and it is problematic, to the point that ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "It is a solecism (*lahn*) of the scribes of the codex." Its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) according to the scholars of Basra is that it is a subject (مبتدأ), and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: "and the Sabians likewise." It is fronted in intention, though it is meant to be deferred. Some of the Kufans permitted that it be conjoined to the position of the subject of *inna* (اسم إن). It has also been said that *inna* here means "yes" (بمعنى نعم), and what follows it is in the nominative as a subject, but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 71:

﴿And they thought there would be no trial (fitnah)﴾, i.e., affliction and testing. It is also read as ﴿takūna﴾ with a nominative (raf') reading, where "an" is the lightened form of "an" from the heavy (thaqilah) form, and with an accusative (nasb) reading, where it is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) "an". ﴿So they became blind and deaf﴾, an expression for their persistence in opposition and disobedience. ﴿Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness﴾. It has been said that this repentance was the restoration of their kingship and their return to Bayt al-Maqdis after they had been expelled from it; then they were expelled a second time, and their condition was never restored. It has also been said that the repentance refers to the sending of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), and it has been said that it refers to the sending of Muḥammad (ﷺ). ﴿Then many of them﴾ is a substitute (badl) for the pronoun in ʿamū wa-ṣammū, or it is the subject (fāʿil) according to the dialect of "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me), and the substitution is more preferred and more eloquent.

﴿And the Messiah said﴾, the verse: a refutation of the Christians and a denial of their claims. ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. It may be part of the Messiah's speech, or part of Allah's speech.

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger﴾, the verse: a refutation of those who made him a god. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾, meaning one who is extremely truthful (ṣiddīqa), or from taṣdīq (affirming the truth). Describing her with this attribute and not with prophethood repels the view of those who say she was a prophetess. ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ is an argument (istidlāl) that the two of them are not gods, because they need food, which only a created, dependent being needs. Whoever is like this is not a god, because God is exalted above the attribute of createdness (ḥudūth) and above everything that befalls humans. It is also said that His statement ﴿they both used to eat food﴾ is a kināya (an allusive expression) for the deficiency of humanity. There is no necessity to take the wording away from its apparent meaning, because the proof stands on both readings.

﴿Then look﴾: the particle thumma (ثُمَّ) was used to indicate the disparity between the two matters, and to express amazement at their disbelief after the signs have been made clear.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 76–77:

﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?"﴾ (the verse): It is an establishment of proof against those who worship Jesus and his mother, while they possess neither harm nor benefit. ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess (ghuluww) in your religion"﴾: it is addressed to the Christians, and ghuluww means exceeding the limits (ifrat). The cause of this is the disbelief of the Christians. ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people﴾: it has been said that they are their leaders in the religion of Christianity, who were upon misguidance concerning Jesus and who misled many people, and then they went astray by their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that they are the Jews. The first view is more likely (arjah) for two reasons. The first is that misguidance is a constant attribute of the Christians; do you not see the words of the Most High: ﴿and not of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7]. The second is that it is far-fetched to forbid the Christians from following the Jews, given the enmity and discord that lies between them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 76–77:

﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?"﴾ (the verse): It is an establishment of proof against those who worship Jesus and his mother, while they possess neither harm nor benefit. ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess (ghuluww) in your religion"﴾: it is addressed to the Christians, and ghuluww means exceeding the limits (ifrat).
