Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 82:

﴿لَتَجِدَنَّ أَشَدَّ ٱلنَّاسِ عَدَاوَةً﴾ "You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity [toward the believers]" – the Qur'an, "etc." (al-ayah): a report about the intensity of the enmity of the Jews and the idol-worshippers toward the Muslims. ﴿وَلَتَجِدَنَّ أَقْرَبَهُمْ مَّوَدَّةً﴾ "And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection" – "etc." (al-ayah): a report that the Christians are closer to the affection of the Muslims, and this matter remains until the end of time, so every Jew is intensely hostile to Islam and plots against its people. ﴿ذٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ مِنْهُمْ قِسِّيسِينَ وَرُهْبَاناً﴾ "That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban)" – this is the reason (ta'lil) for the nearness of their affection. The qissis (qissis) is the learned scholar, and the rahib (rahib) is the worshipper.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 83:

﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾ — the verse (ayah) concerns the Negus (al-Najashi), and the delegation he sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who were seventy men. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, and they wept just as the Negus wept when Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) recited to him Surat Maryam. Al-Suhayli said: it was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, who were twenty Christian men; when they heard the Qur'an they wept. ﴿Because of the truth they have recognized﴾ — the first "min" (because of) indicates causation, and the second "min" is explanatory of the genus (min al-jins). ﴿They say: "Our Lord, we have believed"﴾ — that is, in the Qur'an as coming from Allah. ﴿So write us among the witnesses﴾ — that is, among the Muslims, and likewise among the righteous people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 84–88:

﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not believe in God﴾: a rebuke directed at themselves, or an argument addressed to others. ﴿And we hope﴾: al-Zamakhshari said, "The waw is for the circumstantial (hal)." Ibn 'Atiyya said, "It is for conjoining one sentence to another, not for conjoining one verb to another." ﴿Do not forbid the good things that God has made lawful for you﴾: its occasion was that some of the Companions were overcome by fear of God, to the point that some of them forbade themselves women, some forbade themselves sleeping at night, some forbade themselves eating meat, and some of them resolved to become celibate or to wander through the earth. ﴿And do not transgress﴾: that is, do not go to excess in making things strict for yourselves beyond what has been prescribed for you. ﴿And eat﴾: that is, enjoy the lawful foods, and [enjoy] women and other things. The eating was singled out for mention only because it is the greatest of human needs.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 5, verse 89:**

﴿For idle oaths﴾ has been discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqara. ﴿For what you have bound by oaths﴾, meaning for what you intended to bind by oath with your intention. It is also read as ʿaqadtum (with light emphasis), and as ʿaqadtum (with an alif). ﴿Feeding ten needy people﴾. Specifying that they be needy (miskin) is evidence that feeding a rich person does not suffice for expiation (kaffara). If someone feeds a rich person out of ignorance, it does not suffice according to the well-known position of the school. Malik also stipulated that they be free and Muslim, but there is nothing in the verse that indicates this. ﴿From the average of what you feed your families﴾. Scholars differed over whether this "average" (tawassut) refers to quantity or to type, and the wording allows both interpretations. As for quantity, Malik said that in Medina one feeds one mudd (a unit of measure) by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), and elsewhere, the average amount of satiety. Al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Qasim said that one mudd suffices everywhere. Abu Hanifa said that if one provides them with lunch and dinner, that suffices. As for type, scholars differed over whether one should feed from the food of one's own household or from the food of the people of one's locality. According to the second interpretation, the meaning of the verse is: "from the average of what you, O people, feed your families in general," whereas according to the first, the address is specific to the one making expiation. ﴿Or clothing them﴾. Many scholars said that one garment for a needy person suffices, since it is called clothing (kiswa). Malik said that only what is sufficient for prayer suffices: for a man one garment, and for a woman a shift and a head-covering (khimar). ﴿Or freeing a slave﴾. Malik stipulated that the slave be a believer, since in the expiation for killing it is qualified as such, so he applied this unqualified (mutlaq) wording to that qualified (muqayyad) wording. Abu Hanifa permitted the freeing of any slave for expiation here, on the basis of the unrestricted wording here. Malik also stipulated that the slave be free of defects, but there is nothing in the wording that indicates this. ﴿But whoever does not find﴾, meaning whoever does not possess what would free a slave, nor what would feed, nor what would clothe, then he must fast three days. The three options are optional (takhyir), and fasting is ordered after them for whoever lacks them. According to Malik, this means one who has no surplus over his own sustenance and that of his dependents for that day. ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾, meaning when you swear and fear or intend to break them. Scholars differed over whether it is permissible to precede the expiation before breaking the oath or not. ﴿And guard your oaths﴾, meaning keep them, so that you fulfill them and do not break them. It was also said: guard them by expiating them when you break them. It was further said: guard them by not forgetting them out of disregard for them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 90–91:

﴿Wine (khamr) and gambling (maysir)﴾ — mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah [2:219].

﴿And idols (anṣab) and divining arrows (azlam)﴾ — both mentioned at the beginning of this surah.

﴿Rijs (filth)﴾ — linguistically, it means everything disliked and blameworthy. It is also used to mean impurity (najas) and to mean prohibited (ḥaram). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning of rijs is wrath (sukhṭ).

﴿So avoid it﴾ — this is an explicit text on prohibition. The pronoun refers back to rijs, which is the predicate describing all the things mentioned.

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾ — this is a condemnation of wine and gambling, a mention of some of their defects, and a justification for their prohibition. Enmity arose between people during the time of the Companions because of their drinking of wine before it was prohibited, and it is said that this was the occasion of the revelation of the verse.

﴿So will you not desist?﴾ — this is a command to stop, containing a warning and a threat. That is why ʿUmar, when it was revealed, said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

﴿So will you not desist?﴾ — this is a command to stop, containing a warning and a threat. That is why ʿUmar, when it was revealed, said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾. Regarding this verse there are two interpretations. The first is that when the prohibition of wine was revealed, some of the Companions (ṣaḥābah, the Prophet's companions) said: "What about those among us who died while drinking it?" So the verse was revealed to inform them that there is no blame on whoever drank it before the prohibition, because he did not disobey Allah by drinking it at that time. The second is that the meaning is the lifting of blame from the believers for what they have eaten of foods, provided they avoid what is unlawful among them. Based on this, ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) took it this way when he said to Qudāmah: "If you fear Allah, you will avoid what He has forbidden to you." Qudāmah had drunk wine and argued with this verse to have the blame lifted from him, so ʿUmar said: "You have misinterpreted."

﴿When they fear Allah, believe, and do good deeds﴾ (the verse continues). It was said that taqwā (God-consciousness) is repeated for emphasis. It was also said that the first level is avoiding shirk (associating partners with Allah), the second is avoiding sins, and the third is avoiding what is not harmful, out of caution against what is harmful. It was also said that the first taqwā refers to the past, the second to the present, and the third to the future.

﴿And do good (iḥsān)﴾. This may mean doing good to people, or excellence (iḥsān) in obedience to Allah, which is muraqabah (constant awareness of Allah). This second meaning is more likely correct, because it is a rank above taqwā, and therefore it was mentioned in the third instance, which is the ultimate goal. For this reason the Sufis said: "The stations are three: the station of Islam, then the station of Iman (faith), then the station of Iḥsān."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 94:

﴿Surely Allah will test you with something of the game﴾ meaning: He will test your obedience from your disobedience by means of the game that appears to you while you are in ihram and within the Sacred Precinct (al-haram). Game was among the livelihoods of the Arabs and was in common use among them, so they were tested by abstaining from it, just as the Children of Israel were tested with the fish on the Sabbath. He made it little in His saying ﴿of the game﴾ to indicate that it is not among the great trials, but is among the matters one can be patient in abstaining from. ﴿That your hands and your spears can reach﴾. Mujahid said: what the hands can reach are the young birds and the eggs, and what cannot flee; and what the spears can reach are the large game. The apparent meaning is the generality of this specification. ﴿So that Allah may know﴾ meaning: He will know it with a knowledge by which the proof is established, and that is when it manifests in existence. ﴿Whoever transgresses﴾ meaning: by killing the game while in ihram. ﴿For him is a painful punishment﴾ here refers to the Hereafter.

**Qur'an 5:95:** ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.﴾ *Muhrimun* means those who have entered into ihram (the state of consecration for pilgrimage) or who are within the Haram (the sacred precinct). The word *sayd* (game) here is general, but the hadith has specified from it: the crow, the kite, the mouse, the scorpion, and the rabid dog. Malik extended "the rabid dog" to include every predator and other creature that harms people. Al-Shafi'i analogized from these five to every animal whose meat is not eaten. The word *sayd* covers both what has been hunted and what has not yet been hunted but is of a kind that is normally hunted. The prohibition here is on killing, both before and after the animal is caught. The prohibition on hunting itself is derived from His words: ﴿The game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram﴾ and ﴿whoever of you kills it intentionally﴾. The implication of the verse is that the compensation for game applies to one who kills intentionally, not to one who does so forgetfully. This is the view of the Ahl al-Zahir (the literalist school). The majority of jurists said that the intentional and the forgetful are equal in the obligation of compensation. They then differed concerning His words *muta'ammidan* (intentionally), in three opinions. The first: the word was mentioned so that the threat in His words ﴿whoever returns, God will take vengeance upon him﴾ may be attached to it, since there is no threat for the forgetful. The second: the compensation for the forgetful is by analogy with the intentional. The third: the compensation for the intentional is established by the Qur'an, and the compensation for the forgetful is established by the Sunnah.

﴿Then the compensation is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾. The meaning is: then upon him is a compensation. It has been read as *jaza'u* (with *jaza'* in the construct) added to *mithlu* (like), which is the idafa of the verbal noun to its direct object. It has been said that *mithl* is redundant, as in your saying: "I honor the like of you," meaning "I honor you." It has also been read as *fa-jaza'un* with tanwin, and *mithlu* in the nominative, as a substitute or an adjective. *Al-na'am* (livestock) refers specifically to camels, cattle, and sheep.

According to Malik and al-Shafi'i, the meaning of the verse is that whoever kills game while in ihram owes, as a ransom, something resembling that game in form and appearance. So for an ostrich, a *badanah* (a camel fit for sacrifice) is due; for a wild donkey, a cow; for a gazelle, a sheep. On this view, the likeness is in form and measure. If there is no like of it, then he feeds the poor or fasts. The position of Abu Hanifa is that *al-mithl* means the value: the slain game is assessed, and the slayer is given the choice between giving its value in charity or buying with that value livestock to offer as a sacrifice.

﴿Judged by two men of justice among you﴾. This verse implies that arbitration is a condition for paying the compensation, and there is no disagreement about this. If someone pays the compensation before it has been judged, he must repeat it after the judgment, except for the pigeons of Makkah, for which two arbiters are not needed. This is the view of Malik. According to Malik, arbitration is obligatory both in cases where the Companions issued a ruling and in cases where they did not, on the basis of the general wording of the verse. Al-Shafi'i held that it suffices to rely on what the Companions ruled.

﴿As an offering﴾: its apparent meaning requires that what is given from the livestock as compensation for game must be something that may be offered as a sacrifice. This is the *jadha'* (a young sheep of the sheep kind, in its first year) from sheep, and the *thaniyy* (an animal of the second year or older) from the other kinds. Al-Shafi'i said: one gives the like in meat, and age is not a condition.

﴿Reaching the Ka'bah﴾. He did not mean the Ka'bah itself, but the Haram. It implies that the compensation is treated as the sacrificial offering is treated, by driving it from the non-sacred area (*al-hill*) into the sacred area (*al-haram*). Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: if he buys it within the Haram, that suffices.

﴿Or expiation: feeding the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾. The Exalted has enumerated what is due for the killing of game by one in ihram. He first mentioned the compensation from livestock, then the food, then the fasting. The position of Malik and the majority is that these are optional (*al-takhyir*), which is what the particle *aw* (or) indicates. The position of Ibn 'Abbas is that they are in a fixed order (*al-tartib*). God has not specified here the quantity of food, so the scholars held that the compensation should be measured in livestock, since they differed on how the measure is to be estimated. Malik said: the slain game itself is assessed in grain or in dirhams, and then the dirhams are converted into grain, so one looks at how much grain or how many dirhams it would be worth while alive. Some of Malik's companions said: the game is assessed in food, that is, one asks how much food the game would satisfy in terms of persons, and then one gives food in the amount that would satisfy them. Al-Shafi'i said: the game itself is not assessed; rather, its like is assessed, which is the compensation owed by the one who killed it.

﴿Or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾. The demonstrative *dhalika* (that) may refer to the food, which is the better reading because it is closer, or to the game. There was disagreement about converting food into fasting. Malik said: each *mudd* (a measure of grain) counts as one day. Abu Hanifa said: each two *mudds* count as one day. It was also said: each *sa'* (a larger measure) counts as one day. No compensation, feeding, or fasting is due except upon killing the game, not upon merely catching it without killing, since the verse says: "whoever kills it." In every case, the ruling of the two arbiters is a condition. The reason God did not mention the quantity for fasting and feeding is that it is sufficient to have mentioned it in the compensation.

﴿That he may taste the consequence of his deed﴾. *Al-dhawq* (tasting) is used here metaphorically, since its literal meaning is by the sense of the tongue. *Al-wabal* means the evil outcome, and here it refers to the expiation that has become binding on him.

﴿God has pardoned what is past﴾, that is, what you did in the pre-Islamic period of ignorance (*al-jahiliyyah*) by killing game in the Haram.

﴿But whoever returns, God will take vengeance upon him﴾, that is, whoever returns to killing game while in ihram after the prohibition of that. God will take vengeance upon him either by making expiation obligatory upon him, or by punishing him in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 96:

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾ By this verse, God has made the game of the sea lawful for both the one in a state of ihram (ihram: the sacred state of pilgrimage) and the one not in that state. Here "game" (ṣayd) means the thing hunted, and "the sea" (al-baḥr) means a large body of water, whether salt or fresh, such as pools and the like. Its "food" (ṭaʿām) is that which floats on the water and that which the sea casts up, because that is food and not game. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its food is what has been salted and preserved. ﴿A provision for you and for the travelers﴾ The address "for you" (lakum) is to those present at the sea, and "the travelers" (al-sayyara) are those on journeys, meaning it is a provision by which you and they sustain yourselves. ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in a state of ihram﴾ The word "game" (ṣayd) here may be understood as the verbal noun (the act of hunting), or as the thing hunted, or as both. From this arises the ruling that whatever the one in ihram hunts, he may not eat of it in any way. Disagreement arose concerning what someone other than him hunts. If a lawful person (ḥalāl) hunts, it has been said: it is permissible for the one in ihram to eat it; and it has been said: it is not permissible if it was hunted for a person in ihram. All three opinions are transmitted from Malik. If a forbidden person (muḥrim) hunts, it is not permissible for anyone else to eat it according to Malik, unlike al-Shafiʿi.

﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people﴾, meaning a matter by which people are sustained in security and benefit. It was also said: it is a place of standing for the rites (al-manasik). The word "the people" here is general. It was also said that it refers specifically to the Arabs, because they were the ones who revered the Ka'bah.

﴿And the sacred month﴾: he means the category of the four sacred months, because they would refrain from fighting during them.

﴿And the offering﴾: he means that it is a protection for the one who drives it, because it is known that he is engaged in worship and has not come for war.

﴿And the garlands﴾: when a man set out intending the Hajj, he would wear around his neck something from the samur trees, and when he returned he would wear something from the trees of the Haram, so that it would be known that he was in a state of worship, and no one would harm him in any way. Thus "the garlands" here refers to what the muhrim (the one in ihram) wears of the trees. It was also said: he means the garlands of the offering. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Allah established these matters for the people in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), and He made them stricter in Islam.

﴿That﴾: the reference is to Allah's establishing these matters as a means of standing for the people. The meaning is that Allah made that so that you may know that Allah knows the details of all matters.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 100–102:

﴿Not equal are the wicked and the good﴾ This is a general expression covering all matters: earnings, deeds, people, and other things. ﴿Do not ask about things which, if they were made known to you, would distress you﴾. It was said that the cause of its revelation was the question of ʿAbdullah ibn Ḥudhafah: "Who is my father?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Your father is Ḥudhafah." Another man said: "Where is my father?" He said: "In the Fire." It was also said that its cause was that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has prescribed for you the Ḥajj, so perform it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?" He remained silent. They repeated the question, and he said: "No. And if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory." According to the first explanation, ﴿it would distress you﴾ refers to being informed of what does not please you; according to the second, it refers to being burdened with what is hard for you. This second reading is strengthened by his saying (ﷺ), ﴿Allah has pardoned it﴾, meaning: He remained silent about mentioning it and did not hold you accountable for it, like his saying (ﷺ): "Allah has pardoned the zakat on horses." It was also said that the meaning of ﴿Allah has pardoned it﴾ is: He has pardoned you for your earlier question, so do not return to it. ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made known to you﴾. This contains the sense of a warning against asking: as if He said, "Do not ask; and if you do ask, what displeases you will be made manifest to you." By "when the Qur'an is being revealed" is meant the time of revelation. ﴿A people before you asked about them﴾. The pronoun in "asked about them" refers to the matter indicated by "do not ask," which is a verbal noun (maṣdar); for this reason it is not followed by ʿan, as in His saying "if you ask about them" is. The reason is that the Children of Israel used to seek rulings from their prophets about things; when they were commanded to do them, they abandoned them and perished. Thus, disbelief here is an expression for abandoning what they were commanded.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 103:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahira (a she-camel left to roam freely), nor sa'iba (a free-roaming camel), nor wasila (a she-camel or sheep that gives birth to twins of both sexes), nor ham (a stallion camel left unridden).﴾

When people asked about these practices of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), namely whether they were to be venerated in honour of the Ka'ba and the offerings (al-hady), Allah informed them that He had not made any of that for His servants, meaning He had not prescribed it for them. Rather, the disbelievers devised it. As for the bahira, it is the form فعيلة in the sense of مفعولة, from بَحَر meaning "to split." When a she-camel gave birth to ten offspring, they would split her ear and leave her to graze, and no benefit was taken from her. As for the sa'iba, a man would say, "If I return from my journey or recover from my illness, then my she-camel is sa'iba," and it was like the bahira in that no benefit was taken from it. As for the wasila, when a she-camel gave birth to a male and a female in one birth, they would say, "The she-camel has joined (وصلت) her brother," and they would not slaughter her. As for the ham, when a stallion camel had sired ten offspring, they would say, "His back has been protected (قد حمى ظهره)," so he would not be ridden and nothing would be loaded upon him.

﴿But those who disbelieved fabricate lies against Allah﴾, meaning they lie against Him by forbidding what Allah has not forbidden.

﴿And most of them do not reason.﴾ Those who fabricate lies against Allah are those who invented the prohibition of these things, and those who do not reason are their followers who imitated them blindly (المقلدون).

"They say: 'Sufficient for us is that upon which we found our fathers.'" That is, the religion of our fathers suffices us. "Even though their fathers..." Al-Zamakhshari said: the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has entered upon it; it is as if it were said: "Does it suffice them even though their fathers did not understand, nor were they guided?" Ibn 'Atiyya said: the alif of interrogation (alif al-tawqif [al-istifham]) entered upon the waw of conjunction (waw al-'atf), and al-Zamakhshari's view is better in meaning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 105:

﴿Upon you is your own self; no one who has strayed can harm you once you are guided.﴾ It has been said that it is abrogated (naskh) by the command to enjoin good and forbid evil (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar). It has also been said that it is addressed to the Muslims descended from those who prohibited the baḥīrah and its counterparts, as if it says: the straying of your forefathers will not harm you once you are guided. The correct view concerning it is what has been transmitted from Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'Enjoin good and forbid evil; but when you see stinginess obeyed, desire followed, worldliness preferred, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion, then keep to your own self and leave the common people (awamm) to themselves.'" Similar to this is the statement of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "This is not the time of this verse. Speak the truth as long as it is accepted from you; but if it is rejected by you, then upon you is your own self."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 106–108:

﴿O you who believe, when death approaches one of you, let there be a testimony between you: two just witnesses﴾.

Makki said: This verse is the most difficult verse of the Qur'an in terms of its grammatical analysis (i'rab), its meaning, and its rulings. We will explain its meaning in general terms, then explain its rulings and grammatical analysis in detail. Its occasion of revelation was that two men went out to Syria, and another man went out with them for trade. He fell ill on the way, so he wrote a document recording everything he had with him, placed it among his goods, and charged the two men to deliver his baggage to his heirs. He died, and the two men arrived at Medina and handed the baggage to his heirs. They found in it his document, but they were missing some items he had recorded. They asked the two men, who said: "We do not know; this is what we received." The heirs brought them before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear an oath. The matter remained for a period, then a large silver vessel was found. It was said to the one in whose possession it was found: "From where did you get this?" He said: "I bought it from so-and-so and so-and-so," meaning the two men. The matter was then referred to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered two men from the heirs of the deceased to swear an oath; they swore and were entitled (to the property).

So the meaning of the verse is: When death approaches one of you during a journey, then let him call two just witnesses to testify concerning what he has with him. If doubt arises about their testimony, the two swear that they have not lied and have not altered anything. If it is then discovered that they lied or betrayed, two men from the heirs of the deceased shall swear, and the two witnesses shall be made to pay what was found in their possession.

Grammatical analysis of the verse: "شهادة بينكم" (testimony among you) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "اثنان" (two). The estimated reading is: "the testimony among you is the testimony of two," or "the one establishing testimony among you is two." "إذا حضر" means: when it approaches, i.e., draws near. The governing element of "إذا" is the verbal noun "شهادة" (testimony). This is on the basis that "إذا" has the function of "حين" (when) and requires no response clause (jawab). It is permissible for it to be conditional, in which case its response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, for the meaning is: "When death approaches one of you, one should call witnesses at the time of the bequest." The governing element of "حين" (at the time) is "حضر" (approached), and it may be a substitute (badal) for "إذا." "﴿ذَوَا عَدْلٍ﴾" (two just men) is an attribute of the witnesses "منكم" (from among you), "﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾" (or two others from outside your number). It was said: "منكم" means from your clan and relatives, and "من غيركم" means from outside the clan and kinship. The majority said: "منكم" means from among the Muslims, and "من غيركم" means from among the disbelievers, if no Muslim is available. Then scholars differed on this: is it abrogated by His saying: "And call to witness two just men from among you," so that the testimony of disbelievers is never permissible? This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority. Or is it muhkam (not abrogated), and the testimony of disbelievers is permissible in the case of travel? This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. "﴿إِنْ أَنتُمْ ضَرَبْتُمْ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ﴾" (if you travel in the land) means: if you journey. The response to "إن" is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the meaning is: "If you travel in the land and the calamity of death befalls you, then the testimony among you is the testimony of two." "﴿تَحْبِسُونَهُمَا﴾" (you detain them both): Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said it is an attribute of "آخران" and that a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) intervenes between the attribute and the thing described, with His saying "إن أنتم..." up to "الموت," in order to convey that turning to two others from outside the community is permitted only out of necessity, when travelling in the land and death occurs during the journey. Al-Zamakhshari said: "تحبسونهما" is a resumed statement (isti'naf).

"﴿مِن بَعْدِ ٱلصَّلاَةِ﴾" (after the prayer). The majority said: it is the 'Asr prayer, and the definite article is for previous reference, because it is the time when people gather, and after it the Prophet ﷺ commanded oaths, saying: "Whoever swears an oath over a commodity after the 'Asr prayer..." and the administering of oaths after it was known among them. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the prayer of the disbelievers in their religion, because they do not hold the 'Asr prayer in esteem. "﴿فَيُقْسِمَانِ بِٱللَّهِ﴾" (then they swear by Allah), i.e., they take an oath. The position of the majority is that the requirement of oath-taking for the witnesses is abrogated, though 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari did administer oaths to them. "﴿إِنِ ٱرْتَبْتُمْ﴾" (if you doubt) means: if you are uncertain about their truthfulness or trustworthiness. This phrase is a parenthetical clause between the oath and what is sworn to, and the response to "إن" is omitted, indicated by "يقسمان." "﴿لاَ نَشْتَرِي بِهِ ثَمَناً﴾" (we will not sell it for any price) is what is sworn to. The pronoun in "به" refers to the oath, and in "كان" to the one for whom the oath is made. That is: we will not exchange the validity of the oath by Allah for any worldly goods, i.e., we will not swear falsely by Allah for the sake of wealth, even if the one for whom we swear is a relative of ours, because people naturally incline toward their relatives. "﴿وَلاَ نَكْتُمُ شَهَادَةَ ٱللَّهِ﴾" (nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah) means: the testimony that Allah commanded to be preserved and rendered, and its attribution to Allah is to exalt it. "﴿فَإِنْ عُثِرَ عَلَىٰ أَنَّهُمَا ٱسْتَحَقَّآ إِثْماً﴾" (then if it is discovered that the two deserved sin) means: if it becomes known afterwards that they committed what necessitates sin; sin here is lying and betrayal, and "استحقاقه" means being qualified to be described by it. "﴿فَآخَرَانِ يَقُومَانِ مَقَامَهُمَا﴾" (then two others shall stand in their place) means: two from among the heirs of the deceased, who stand in place of the two witnesses in the oath. "﴿مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْتَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ﴾" (from among those against whom it was deserved) means: from among those against whom sin or property was deserved, i.e., those wronged by them, who are the heirs of the deceased. "﴿ٱلأَوْلَيَٰنِ﴾" (the two nearest) is the dual of "أولى" in the sense of "أحق" (more entitled): i.e., those more entitled to the testimony because of their knowledge of it, and more entitled to the property because of their kinship. It is in the nominative, being the predicate of an implied subject whose estimate is "هما الأوليان" (they are the two nearest), or a delayed subject whose estimate is "الأوليان آخران يقومان" (the two nearest, two others who stand), or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "يقومان." Al-Farisi prohibited attributing "استحق" to "الأوليان," but Ibn 'Atiyya permitted it. As for the reading "استحق" with a fatha on the ta' and ha' (in the active voice), "الأوليان" is the subject of "استحق," and the meaning of "استحق" on this reading is taking the property and taking possession of it; and "الأوليان" on this reading are the two witnesses whose betrayal became evident, i.e., "the most deserving" of being made to swear, of being rebuked, and of being disgraced. It is also read "الأولين," the plural of "أول," in the genitive as an attribute of "الذين استحق عليهم," or in the accusative by an implied verb; they are described as "first" because they precede outsiders in entitlement to the property and in the truthfulness of testimony. "﴿فَيُقْسِمَانِ بِٱللَّهِ لَشَهَٰدَتُنَا أَحَقُّ مِن شَهَٱدَتِهِمَا﴾" (then they both swear by Allah: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony") means: these two others swear that their testimony is more worthy, i.e., more correct, than the testimony of the two witnesses whose betrayal became evident. "﴿إِنَّا إِذاً لَّمِنَ ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾" (indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers) means: if we transgress, then we are among the wrongdoers; this is a form of disavowal, like the statement of the first: "Indeed, then we would be among the sinners." "﴿ذٰلِكَ أَدْنَىٰ أَن يَأْتُواْ بِٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهَآ﴾" (that is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form) means: the reference of "ذلك" is to the ruling that took place in this case; "أدنى" means "أقرب" (closer); "على وجهها" means as it occurred, without alteration or change. Or [it means] "أو يخافوا" (or they fear): "﴿أَن تُرَدَّ أَيْمَانٌ بَعْدَ أَيْمَٰنِهِمْ﴾" (that oaths will be repeated after their oaths), i.e., they fear that others will swear after them and thereby expose them.

﴿O you who believe, when death approaches one of you, let there be a testimony between you: two just witnesses﴾.

Makki said: This verse is the most difficult verse of the Qur'an in terms of its grammatical analysis (i'rab), its meaning, and its rulings. We will explain its meaning in general terms, then explain its rulings and grammatical analysis in detail. Its occasion of revelation was that two men went out to Syria, and another man went out with them for trade. He fell ill on the way, so he wrote a document recording everything he had with him, placed it among his goods, and charged the two men to deliver his baggage to his heirs. He died, and the two men arrived at Medina and handed the baggage to his heirs. They found in it his document, but they were missing some items he had recorded. They asked the two men, who said: "We do not know; this is what we received." The heirs brought them before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear an oath. The matter remained for a period, then a large silver vessel was found. It was said to the one in whose possession it was found: "From where did you get this?" He said: "I bought it from so-and-so and so-and-so," meaning the two men. The matter was then referred to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered two men from the heirs of the deceased to swear an oath; they swore and were entitled (to the property).

The governing element of "إذا" is the verbal noun "شهادة" (testimony). This is on the basis that "إذا" has the function of "حين" (when) and requires no response clause (jawab). The governing element of "حين" (at the time) is "حضر" (approached), and it may be a substitute (badal) for "إذا." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 109:

﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾ It is the Day of Resurrection. The adverbial phrase (zarf) is governed by a suppressed verb, meaning: "What answer did the nations give you, of belief and disbelief, obedience and disobedience?" The purpose of this question is to rebuke those among the nations who disbelieved and to establish the proof against them. The phrase "mā ajabtum" (what did you answer) is in the accusative as the infinitive of its verb, i.e., it is the object of a verbal noun (masdar). Had the answer been intended, it would have been said "bi-mā ajabtum" (with what did you answer). ﴿They will say, "We have no knowledge."﴾ They said this out of courtesy toward Allah, so they left the knowledge to Him. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is, "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us." It was also said that the meaning is: our knowledge is insignificant beside Your knowledge. This is strengthened by His saying, ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen,﴾ for whoever knows the hidden matters, the apparent matters are not concealed from him. It was also said that they were bewildered from answering because of the terror of that Day, but this is far-fetched, since the Prophets will be secure on that Day. And it was said that they intended by this to rebuke the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 110:

﴿إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ It is possible that "idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "yawma yajmaʿu" (the day when Allah gathers the messengers), and that this speech takes place on the Day of Resurrection. Or the governing element (al-ʿamil) of "idh" is an implied verb, and in this case the speech may be in this world or on the Day of Resurrection. If we take it to be the Day of Resurrection, then his words "qala" (said) carry the sense of "yaqulu" (says). The explanation of the wording of this verse has already been given in Surat Al ʿImran.

﴿فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا﴾ The feminine pronoun refers to the "kaf" (the particle "ka" in "ka-hayʾati"), because it is a description of the form (hayʾa). Likewise the pronoun in "takunu" (it becomes). Likewise the masculine pronoun mentioned in his words in Al ʿImran, "fa-yanfukhu fihi" (then he breathes into it), also refers to the "kaf," since it carries the meaning of "mithl" (like). If you wish, you may say that in both places it refers to the omitted noun that is described by the phrase "ka-hayʾati," so its estimated form in the feminine is "ṣūra" (form), and in the masculine is "shakhṣan" (a figure), "khalqan" (a creature), or something similar. It has also been said that the feminine refers to the "hayʾa" (form) and the masculine refers to the "ṭayr" (bird) and the "ṭīn" (clay), but this is weak in meaning.

﴿بِإِذْنِي﴾ He repeated it with every miracle, as a refutation of those who attributed divinity (rububiyya) to ʿIsa.

﴿وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ عَنكَ﴾ meaning the Jews, when they resolved to kill him, so Allah raised him up to Himself.

﴿And when I inspired﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, so it is among the blessings Allah bestowed upon Jesus. The word "inspiration" (wahy) here may mean inspiration of inner suggestion (ilham) or inspiration of speech. ﴿And bear witness﴾ may be addressed to Allah the Exalted or to Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿When Allah said: O Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. Their calling him by his name is evidence that they did not venerate him as the Muslims venerate Muhammad (ﷺ), for they did not call him by his name but would say: "O Messenger of God, O Prophet of God." Their saying "son of Mary" is evidence that they held the correct belief about him, in attributing him to a mother without a father, unlike what the Christians believed.

﴿Is your Lord able﴾: the apparent meaning of this expression is that they doubted Allah the Exalted's power to send down the table spread (al-ma'idah). Al-Zamakhshari adopted this view and said: they were not described by God as believers; rather, their claim is related in their saying "we have believed" (amanna). Ibn 'Atiyya and others said: this is not so, because they did not doubt God's power, but the meaning is "Will your Lord do this, and will He grant their request?" This is the more probable view, because Allah praised the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun) in several places in His Book, although the wording contains an offensive harshness. It has been read as "tasta'(you) [with the feminine second-person prefix] your Lord" in the accusative, meaning "Can you ask your Lord?" This reading does not imply that they doubted. ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) read it this way and said: "The Disciples were too well acquainted with their Lord to say: Is your Lord able?"

The table spread (al-ma'idah) is that upon which there is food; if there is no food upon it, it is called a khiwan (serving tray).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verses 113–115:

﴿They said: "We want to eat from it"﴾: meaning, a meal by which we may gain honour among the people. Their aim was not the craving of the belly.

﴿"and that our hearts may be assured"﴾: meaning, that we may witness the sign, so that our faith becomes certain by necessity and by direct observation, and the doubts that arise in inference do not beset us.

﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us"﴾: its apparent sense supports the view of those who said that they said this before their faith was firmly established. It may also mean: that we may know with a necessary knowledge that admits no doubt.

﴿"and that we may be among its witnesses"﴾: meaning, that we may bear witness to it before those among the people who were not present.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread from heaven"﴾: Jesus responded to their request for the table from Allah. It is narrated that he put on a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, stood up to pray, supplicated, and wept.

﴿"that it may be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us"﴾: it was said: we should take the day of its descent as a festival that recurs every year, for the first of the community and then for those after them. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is that it be a gathering for all of us, the first and the last of us, on the day of its descent specifically, not a recurring festival.

﴿"and a sign from You"﴾: meaning, a proof of my truthfulness.

﴿Allah said: "I am indeed sending it down to you"﴾: Allah responded to them with what they had asked. The table descended upon them; on it were fish and bread. It was also said: olives, dates and pomegranates. Ibn Abbas said: the food of the table would descend upon them wherever they alighted. There are many narrations about the story of the table that are not authentic.

﴿"But whoever among you disbelieves after that, I shall indeed punish him with a punishment"﴾: it is Allah's established practice, may He be exalted, to punish whoever disbelieves after a sign has been requested and given. When some of these people disbelieved, Allah transformed them into swine. Abdullah ibn Amr said: the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are those who disbelieved among the companions of the table, the family of Pharaoh, and the hypocrites...

﴿"and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us"﴾: its apparent sense supports the view of those who said that they said this before their faith was firmly established. It may also mean: that we may know with a necessary knowledge that admits no doubt.

﴿"and that we may be among its witnesses"﴾: meaning, that we may bear witness to it before those among the people who were not present.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread from heaven"﴾: Jesus responded to their request for the table from Allah. It is narrated that he put on a garment of hair and a cloak of hair, stood up to pray, supplicated, and wept.

﴿"that it may be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us"﴾: it was said: we should take the day of its descent as a festival that recurs every year, for the first of the community and then for those after them. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is that it be a gathering for all of us, the first and the last of us, on the day of its descent specifically, not a recurring festival.

﴿"and a sign from You"﴾: meaning, a proof of my truthfulness.

﴿Allah said: "I am indeed sending it down to you"﴾: Allah responded to them with what they had asked. The table descended upon them; on it were fish and bread. It was also said: olives, dates and pomegranates. Ibn Abbas said: the food of the table would descend upon them wherever they alighted. There are many narrations about the story of the table that are not authentic.

﴿"But whoever among you disbelieves after that, I shall indeed punish him with a punishment"﴾: it is Allah's established practice, may He be exalted, to punish whoever disbelieves after a sign has been requested and given. When some of these people disbelieved, Allah transformed them into swine. Abdullah ibn Amr said: the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are those who disbelieved among the companions of the table, the family of Pharaoh, and the hypocrites...

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 5, verse 116:

﴿And when Allah says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people: 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority (al-jumhur) said: this statement will be made by Allah on the Day of Resurrection, before the assembled creation, so that the disbelievers may see the innocence of ʿIsa from what they attributed to him, and know that they were upon falsehood. Al-Suddi said: when Allah raised ʿIsa up to Himself, the Christians said what they said, and claimed that ʿIsa had commanded them to it. Then Allah questioned him about that, and he said: "Glory be to You..." (the verse). According to this, the phrase "idh qal" (when He said) is in the past tense in meaning as it is in form, whereas according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas it carries the meaning of the future.

﴿It is not for me to say what is not the truth.﴾ This is a negation supported by the evidence of reason, since that which is created and originated (al-muhdath) cannot be a god.

﴿If I had said it, You would already know it.﴾ This is an apology and a disavowal of that statement, and he entrusted the knowledge to Allah so that his innocence would become evident, because Allah knew that he had not said that.

﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul.﴾ That is: You know what I know, and I do not know what You know. But he employed the wording in the manner of mushakalah (correspondence of expression), saying "fi nafsik" (in Your soul) in response to his saying "fi nafsi" (in my soul). The rest of his statement is an exaltation of Allah and an informing of what people said in the world.

﴿That you worship﴾: "أن" is an explanatory particle (harf 'ibara wa tafsir), or a verbal particle (masdariyya) substituting for the pronoun in "به" (by it).

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

In this there are two questions.

The first: how did He say "and if You forgive them," when they are disbelievers, and disbelievers are not forgiven? The answer is that the meaning is the submission of the matter to Allah, and that if He punishes or forgives, there is no objection to Him, because the creatures are His servants, and the owner does what he wills in his own dominion. This does not necessitate that forgiveness of the disbelievers occurs; it only implies its permissibility in the wisdom and might of Allah the Exalted. There is a difference between permissibility (al-jawaz) and occurrence (al-wuquʻ). As for the view of those who say that this address is to 'Isa, peace be upon him, at the time Allah raised him to the heavens, then there is no difficulty, because the meaning is "if You forgive them through repentance," and they were then alive, and every living being is subject to repentance.

The second question: what is the connection between His saying "indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise" and His saying "and if You forgive them"? The more fitting thing, with mention of forgiveness, would have been to say "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful."

The answer has three aspects. The first: it appears to me that since the intent was submission to Allah and glorification of Him, His saying ﴿indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ is more fitting, for wisdom requires submission to Him, and might requires glorifying Him. The Exalted in Might is the one who does what He wills, is not overcome by another, and nothing He intends is beyond Him. So the speech entails entrusting the matter to Allah regarding forgiving them or not forgiving them, since He is capable of both by His might, and whichever He does is beautiful by His wisdom.

The second answer is from our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "He only did not say 'the Forgiving, the Merciful' so that there would not be in that an implicit request for their forgiveness. So He limited Himself to submission and entrusting, without asking. For forgiveness is not sought for disbelievers." This is close to what we have said.

The third: our shaykh al-Khatib Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Rushayd related from his teacher, the imam of eloquence of his time, Hazim ibn Hazim, that he used to pause at His saying ﴿and if You forgive them﴾ and make ﴿indeed You are the Exalted in Might﴾ a new sentence (isti'naf), and the answer of "in" in His saying ﴿indeed they are Your servants﴾ is as if He had said: "If You punish them, and if You forgive them, indeed they are Your servants in every state."

This is the day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful. It is a general statement covering all the truthful, and especially Jesus son of Mary, for in it there is an indication of his truthfulness in the speech that God related from him. The rest of the readers, other than Nafi', read "hadha yawmu" (this is a day) with a nominative ending (raf'), as a subject-predicate construction (mubtada' or khabar). Nafi' read it with a accusative ending (nasb), and there are two possible analyses of this:

The first is that yawma be a circumstantial adverb (zarf) governed by "qala" (He said). On this reading, the sentence is not the object of the verb of saying; rather, its object is only "hadha" (this) by itself, and the meaning is: God said, "This account or statement [is] on a day..." This is far-fetched and it removes the splendour of the discourse.

The second is that "hadha" be the subject (mubtada'), with "yawma" in the position of its predicate (khabar), and the governing element being elided, its estimated form being: "This occurs on a day when their truthfulness benefits the truthful." It is not permissible for yawma to be indeclinable (mabni) according to Nafi's reading, because it is then attached to a noun in the declinable (mu'rab) form. This was stated by al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari.
